commons:201237925.summary: Set behind an elaborate gilded Rococo grille, this small wooden statue shows the Virgin seated with the Christ Child held before her, both with long, solemn faces. Venerated for centuries in the abbey church of Remiremont, the 11th-century image has been framed and adorned by later generations as a treasured relic of the abbey's past.
facts: It has been classified as a historic monument (objet classé) since 20 June 1907.
The French heritage database dates the carved wooden statue to the 11th century and notes that it has been dressed in rich fabrics.
According to the Commons record, it is about 68 cm high.
commons:201237925.notes: The photograph shows the statue at a distance behind its gilded grille, so details are hard to make out.
commons:201237925.original_title: Vierge à l'enfant, dite Vierge au Trésor

cur:catacombs2-athens-bcma-good-shepherd.summary: A young shepherd with a round, boyish face and thick hair stands on a small integral base, carrying a sheep across his shoulders and holding its legs with his right hand; two more animals stand at his feet. He wears a short belted tunic and boots, the working dress of a herdsman. Small statuettes like this one, found across the Mediterranean, made the image of Christ the Good Shepherd present in homes and burial places.
facts: According to the museum label recorded on Commons, it comes from Corinth, dates to the 4th century and has the accession number BXM 2.
The Good Shepherd statuette type is also known from Rome, notably the marble figure in the Museo Pio Cristiano of the Vatican Museums.
cur:catacombs2-athens-bcma-good-shepherd.notes: As with all such figures, the shepherd type was shared with pagan art; its Christian meaning is inferred from date and context.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-139-chris.summary: The cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, carrying a cross-staff and attended by angels, places a wreath on the head of the psalmist, accompanied by his men: 'thou hast covered my head in the day of battle'. Below, the wicked sharpen their tongues like serpents and spread a net, and angels hurl torches and brimstone at a band of warriors. The drawing pictures the Lord as the strength of the psalmist's salvation.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
Its text is written in rustic capitals, an archaic script that once led scholars to date the manuscript to the 6th century; the drawings are now recognised as Carolingian.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-139-chris.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:monumental-smm-presentation-in-templ.summary: In a long frieze before a classical temple, the Virgin, richly dressed like a Roman noblewoman, carries the infant Christ towards the aged Simeon, who comes forward with covered hands to receive him, accompanied by Anna, Joseph, angels and a crowd of priests. The scene unfolds in the processional, courtly manner of Late Roman imperial art. Together with the other infancy scenes of the arch, it celebrates Christ's divine kingship in the church built soon after the Council of Ephesus (431).
facts: The triumphal-arch mosaics were made under Pope Sixtus III (432–440), whose dedication SIXTUS EPISCOPUS PLEBI DEI ('Sixtus the bishop to the people of God') is inscribed on the arch.
The basilica's infancy cycle stresses Christ's royal and divine status; Mary is shown in the costume of a Roman empress or noblewoman rather than as a humble mother.

cur:objects-berlin-entry-into-jerusalem-.summary: Beneath an arcade Christ rides sideways on a donkey toward the gate of Jerusalem, followed by his disciples, while the people come out to meet him, children spread garments in his path and a boy climbs a tree to cut branches. The scene is carved in deep relief with many small figures, yet Christ's calm, upright figure remains the clear focus. In the Byzantine cycle of feasts this image announced Palm Sunday and the beginning of the Passion.
facts: The panel was the centre of a triptych; its wings, now lost, would have folded over it to protect the image (type).
The Entry into Jerusalem was one of the Twelve Great Feasts of the Byzantine Church, frequently represented on ivories and icons (type).

cur:objects-douce-ivory-book-cover.summary: In the centre Christ stands triumphant, carrying a cross over his shoulder and a book, trampling the lion, dragon, asp and basilisk. Twelve small surrounding panels narrate episodes from the Gospels, beginning with the Annunciation and Nativity and including miracles of Christ. The composition proclaims the victorious Lord whose earthly life, told around the edges, accomplished the defeat of evil.
facts: Wikipedia's article on Christ treading on the beasts calls it the 'Oxford book cover' and notes its four beasts, the full set named in the Vulgate verse.
The book it covers is MS Douce 176, measuring about 21 × 12 cm.

princeton:24959.summary: Moulded in banded red glass in imitation of a precious stone, this small oval shows Christ on the cross, his body swaying slightly and his head inclined within a halo, between the Virgin at the left and John at the right. Above the arms of the cross are the Greek abbreviations IC XC, 'Jesus Christ'. The use of the Greek monogram points to Byzantine models, made affordable in glass for personal devotion.
facts: It was given to Princeton by Mrs Albert E. McVitty and published among the museum's recent acquisitions in 1955.
princeton:24959.notes: Princeton gives no display date, only the broad range 400–1499 and the label 'Medieval'; the 'A.D. 500–1000' in our data is unsupported. The swaying body and the Virgin-and-John composition suggest Middle Byzantine models (10th century or later), but no firm date can be given; year 950 is a midpoint placeholder.
